title: Finance: Tariffs, Costs and Break-even
summary: Municipal and cellphone tariff systems with sliding scales, comparing options, fixed and variable costs, cost price and selling price, and finding the break-even point from a table, a graph and an equation.

notes.text: A **tariff** is the rate a supplier charges for a service. Tariffs often have a **fixed charge** (paid even if you use nothing) and a **usage charge**. Municipal water and electricity use a **sliding scale** (block tariff): the first units are cheap and each further block costs more, so heavy users pay more per unit.

notes.title: Worked example 1: a sliding-scale bill
notes.problem: The Mokoena household uses 22 kℓ of water in a month. Calculate their bill.
steps: Block 1: the first 6 kℓ are free: R0

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Do **not** multiply all 22 kℓ by the block-3 rate. Only the kilolitres **inside** each block are charged at that block's rate.

To compare tariff options (e.g. a cellphone contract against prepaid), write a formula for each, draw up a table or draw both graphs on the same axes. The point where the graphs cross is where the options cost the same.

notes.title: Worked example 2: contract or prepaid?
notes.problem: Contract: R149 per month including 100 free minutes, then R0,99 per minute. Prepaid: R1,49 per minute. For how many minutes do they cost the same?
steps: Up to 100 minutes the contract costs R149. Prepaid for 100 minutes is R149: the same!
Above 100 minutes: contract = 149 + 0,99 × (minutes − 100), which grows more slowly than prepaid.
notes.answer: They are equal at 100 minutes. For fewer than 100 minutes prepaid is cheaper, and for more than 100 minutes the contract is cheaper.

notes.caption: The mark-up is the amount added to the cost price to make a profit.

notes.text: The **break-even point** is the number of items at which **income = total cost**, so there is no profit and no loss. Sell fewer and the business makes a loss; sell more and it makes a profit.

notes.caption: Break-even graph for the vetkoek stall. The total cost line starts at R600 (the fixed costs) and the income line starts at zero. They cross at 80 vetkoek and R960. To the left of this point the stall makes a loss; to the right it makes a profit.

notes.title: Worked example 3: finding the break-even point
notes.problem: The stall has fixed costs of R600 per month, a variable cost of R4,50 per vetkoek and sells each vetkoek for R12. How many must be sold to break even?
notes.answer: 80 vetkoek (income and costs are both R960).

notes.title: Worked example 4: profit
notes.problem: How much profit does the stall make if it sells 150 vetkoek in a month?

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: A quick check: each item sold above break-even adds (selling price − variable cost) to profit. Here that is R12 − R4,50 = R7,50 per vetkoek, and 70 above break-even × R7,50 = R525.
